query: Why is my real life always waiting on one more thing?

per_question.q: How can I tell whether the condition I am waiting for has quietly changed?
per_question.why: A places the Goethals and Reckman memory finding inside the early section explaining how a condition gets swapped, then gives the dated two-sentence comparison that reveals the change.

per_question.q: What do researchers call a life that is always deferred until later?
per_question.why: B's heading "What Do Researchers Call This, and Where Does the Name Stop?" directly retrieves the answer, followed by the named-term table distinguishing the deferred life plan, anticipated versus experienced utility, and hedonic adaptation.

per_question.q: How do I distinguish a real practical constraint from a moving excuse?
per_question.why: A has the near-verbatim heading "How Do I Distinguish a Real Practical Constraint From a Moving Excuse?" and immediately supplies concrete tests: name the amount, date, document, or person, and check whether it stays fixed.

per_question.q: Why does reaching a milestone feel less life-changing than I predicted?
per_question.why: A uses this question verbatim as a heading and answers it with the milestone-to-floor mechanism, then names anticipated versus experienced utility and hedonic adaptation in the same section.

per_question.q: Is hedonic adaptation really proven, or do some life changes last?
per_question.why: A has a dedicated verbatim heading and a focused evidence review naming the 2011 Luhmann meta-analysis, Headey's 2010 critique, unemployment as a durable effect, and four limits of the panel evidence.

per_question.q: Why do I keep saying I will do it when I have more money even as my savings grow?
per_question.why: Under "Is the Condition About Money, or About Deserving?", A places Easterlin's material-aspirations account and the counterpoint from Stevenson and Wolfers directly beside the explanation of why the target rises with income.

per_question.q: What if the career or trip I keep postponing was never really my goal?
per_question.why: A repeats the question as a heading and adds the motivation-research distinction between an identified goal and one maintained to avoid guilt, alongside the grief-versus-relief diagnostic.

per_question.q: Is putting my life off just another form of procrastination?
per_question.why: A has the question as a dedicated heading and compares the pattern against a three-part research definition of procrastination, including a clear account of which two elements fail and when both patterns can coexist.

per_question.q: What is one small thing I can do this week to test whether I still want the life I postpone?
per_question.why: A uses the full question as its heading and gives two concrete tests immediately below it: compare today's sentence with the one from five years ago, and use one long-saved object on an ordinary day.

per_question.q: How should I stop my teenager from postponing their future?
per_question.why: Neither page directly gives parent-to-teen advice. A is the marginally better citation because its question-framed constraint section explicitly warns against labeling genuine constraints as excuses and provides a fixed-versus-moving test, the safest relevant framework for a parent.

A: Its researcher-label material sits under a milestone heading rather than the highly retrievable researcher-worded heading used by B.
It does not directly address how a parent should respond to a teenager.
B: It lacks dedicated question-matching sections for hedonic adaptation, procrastination, the money-and-growing-savings mechanism, and the postponed-goal question.
It omits A's Goethals and Reckman memory finding, Easterlin and Stevenson-Wolfers income evidence, and the motivation-research model.
It does not directly address how a parent should respond to a teenager.

first_screen: A answers the reader faster overall: although both pages have the same opening answer box, A's body then routes several likely follow-up questions through headings that closely or exactly match the searcher's wording.
provenance: A makes claim origins easier to inspect because named findings are placed inside the sections that answer the relevant question, including Goethals and Reckman on shifting recall, Easterlin and Stevenson-Wolfers on income, and Luhmann and Headey on adaptation.
